name: Loomly
tagline: Plan, approve, and schedule a small team's content calendar

tiers.name: Starter
tiers.limits: 12 social accounts; 3 users; unlimited calendars; 2 social-listening uses/month.
tiers.notes: AI usage is included but the public page labels the allowance only as 'limited' without a number.

tiers.name: Beyond
tiers.limits: 60 social accounts; unlimited users and calendars; 5 social-listening uses/month.
tiers.notes: AI usage is included but the public page labels the allowance only as 'extended' without a number.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: 61+ social accounts; unlimited users and calendars; custom governance, security, and support.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier (15-day no-card trial only)
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual (about 25% lower on annual billing)
pricing.hiddenCosts: AI usage is capped, but the current public page does not publish numeric AI limits; more than 60 social accounts requires Enterprise.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Loomly, plan, approve, and schedule a small team's content calendar. The hard boundary is approval workflow, multi-network publishing, asset library, analytics, and support, plus api access, connector upkeep, and collaboration.
coreLoopDIY: Draft, approve, and schedule a small team's posts, preview them accurately, publish through one official API, and retain a searchable content calendar.
requirements: developer application for one social network
whatYouLose: approval workflow, multi-network publishing, asset library, analytics, and support
moatNotes: API access, connector upkeep, and collaboration
ongoingBurden: OAuth review, API policy changes, media limits, queues, retries, rate limits, webhooks, tokens, and moderation workflows
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Loomly because the scheduler is easy; staying approved and correct across constantly changing social APIs is the subscription. The recurring cost buys OAuth review, API policy changes, media limits, queues, retries, rate limits, webhooks, tokens, and moderation workflows, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Postiz
priorArt.desc: Active open-source social media scheduling platform.

alternatives.name: BrightBean Studio
alternatives.desc: Shared calendars, comments, approvals and publishing, plus an inbox; unusually little is missing.

facts.install: Hosted signup, or clone the repository and deploy with Docker Compose or a supported PaaS.
facts.engines: No model is bundled; its REST API and MCP server connect external agents such as Claude Desktop/Code, Cursor or custom clients.
facts.dataFormat: Hosted data lives in BrightBean's cloud; self-hosted data uses PostgreSQL 16+ with media on local disk or S3-compatible storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: BrightBean's review states, version history and per-network approval polish are less mature than Loomly's team workflow.
facts.setupBlocker: Connecting social networks requires first-party platform developer/OAuth credentials; self-hosting also requires Docker or a PaaS.

alternatives.name: Postiz
alternatives.desc: Teams, comments and scheduling are here; approval polish is thinner and operations are thicker.

facts.install: Hosted signup, or Docker Compose for self-hosting.
facts.engines: Optional AI/media features connect to OpenAI, ElevenLabs, fal.ai, Tavily, KieAI and Transloadit.
facts.dataFormat: PostgreSQL holds application data; Redis and Temporal support jobs; media is stored locally or in Cloudflare R2/S3-compatible storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: Postiz has collaboration basics but thinner approval/versioning controls, while the team must also operate the deployment.
facts.setupBlocker: Hosted use is straightforward; self-hosting requires Docker, social OAuth apps, and a PostgreSQL, Redis and Temporal stack.

alternatives.name: TryPost
alternatives.desc: Workspaces, roles, comments, approvals and a visual calendar; free means hosting the machinery.

facts.install: Hosted signup, or production Docker Compose; a bare-metal installation is also documented.
facts.engines: AI writing can use OpenAI or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint; the deployment template also exposes Anthropic and Gemini keys.
facts.dataFormat: PostgreSQL or MySQL stores app data, Redis handles queues/cache, and media is local or S3-compatible storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: TryPost covers roles and comments but not Loomly's mature approval trail and managed team experience.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting needs a SQL database, Redis, media storage, and separate developer credentials for each social platform.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Base plan and a single-network scheduler DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Loomly in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and one official social-platform API; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: draft, approve, and schedule a small team's posts, preview them accurately, publish through one official API, and retain a searchable content calendar.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Support drafts, scheduled times, queues, campaigns, tags, and a weekly calendar.
Connect exactly one social network using its documented OAuth flow.
Validate character, media, aspect-ratio, and file-size limits before scheduling.
Publish through an idempotent background job with retries and clear failure states.
Store platform post identifiers and refresh publication status without scraping.
Add reusable snippets, local media storage, CSV export, and a token reconnect flow.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out unofficial automation or scraping.
Deliberately leave out multi-network inbox and social listening.
Deliberately leave out agency approvals, white labelling, and enterprise reporting.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
